messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 51
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Tax Inspector
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
  pcl5: 39

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Feeling Tired: Feeling very tired or exhausted, Discomfort: Feeling uncomfortable, Unpredictability: Unpredictable situations
  Threat: False Alarms: I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong, Back to Wall: I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room, Checking Behind: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me
  Memory: Sudden Pieces: Fragments of the memory appear suddenly without warning and then disappear, Memory Gaps: There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try, Uncontrolled Access: The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to
  Negative Appraisals: No Good Ahead: Nothing good can happen to me anymore, Dehumanization: I feel like an object, not like a person, Betrayal: I was betrayed by someone I trusted

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Minh was forty-eight when it happened, though he sometimes felt as though the years before and after had been erased and only that night remained in fragments. He had been with Lina for two years, and he had learned to read the tilt of her jaw, the way her voice would go flat just before she struck. But that evening he had come home late from the office—an audit file had taken longer than expected, and he was tired, so tired that the usual vigilance slipped. She was waiting in the kitchen. The first blow caught him across the cheekbone, and then she was on him, her fists and knees finding his ribs, his thighs, his back. He remembered a white light, the smell of cooking oil, the sound of her breathing. There was a moment when he tried to push her away, and she laughed. Then nothing. A gap. The next thing he knew, he was on the floor, his shirt torn, and she was gone. He never pressed charges. He told himself it was a one-time thing, that he had provoked her, that he was a man and should be able to handle it. But when he looked in the mirror that night he did not see a person; he saw an object, something that had been used and discarded.

The memory did not stay in that night. It arrived in pieces—a flash of her hand, the cold tile against his cheek—without warning, often when he was alone and least expecting it. He would be sitting at his desk at the Revenue Department, reviewing a return, and suddenly the image would push through, and his heart would hammer, and he would have to excuse himself to the restroom. There were long stretches when he could not recall the event at all, not because he was avoiding it, but because the memory simply would not come together; whole minutes were missing, as if someone had cut out a section of film. He would try to reconstruct the sequence, but all he found were gaps, and the effort left him hollow.

What frightened him most, though, was the growing sense that danger had not ended. He began to feel unsafe standing in open rooms; he needed his back against a wall, needed to see every door and every window. At work, he chose a desk in the corner and always sat facing the entrance. He caught himself looking behind him as he walked down the hall, and sometimes he spun around for no reason, certain someone was following. His wife, Thanh, noticed. She asked why he flinched whenever she entered a room quietly. He said it was nothing, but he stopped coming out of the bedroom until he could hear her voice first. At home, he felt most secure with his back to the headboard, scanning the doorway. The false alarms came daily: a car backfiring, a dropped file, a sudden change in a taxpayer’s tone—each time his body braced as if for impact. His chest would tighten, and he would be drenched in sweat before he could reason his way back to calm.

The exhaustion made everything worse. Tiredness became a trigger in itself; if he felt fatigue settling in, he knew the fragments would come more easily, and so he began to avoid rest. He stayed up late, working through spreadsheets, because sleep felt like surrender. He also avoided any situation that felt unpredictable—changing his route to work so that he never encountered a surprise, declining dinner invitations because he could not control the seating arrangement. His supervisor noticed that Minh had stopped taking on new audits, and Thanh grew quiet, unsure how to reach him. He had come to believe that nothing good could happen anymore; the world had shown him what it was, and he was merely moving through it, a shell.

What finally brought him to the clinic was a morning in the office when an intern tapped him on the shoulder from behind. Minh spun around and shoved the young man against a filing cabinet before he knew what he was doing. The intern was shaken, and Minh was asked to take leave. That afternoon, sitting alone in his car, he thought of Lina, of the betrayal, of the feeling that he had been broken and there was nothing left. He called a number Thanh had left on the fridge months ago. He did not know if he could be fixed, but he could not keep living like this—back against the wall, waiting for a blow that never came.
